case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s payment-calculation formula limits a veteran with multiple qualifying periods of service to 36 months of Post-9/11 GI Bill education benefits, or instead allows the veteran to receive up to the 48-month aggregate cap otherwise available when combining different GI Bill programs.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) (Post-9/11 GI Bill election/conversion and benefit-calculation provision) (with the dispute implicating how it interacts with the broader statutory scheme governing aggregate months of entitlement—i.e., the 48-month cap for multiple education benefit programs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that § 3327(d) is being misread to impose an across-the-board 36-month ceiling on veterans who have more than one period of qualifying service and who previously earned Montgomery GI Bill (or other) entitlements; properly interpreted in context, the statute provides a method for calculating Chapter 33 benefits upon an election/transfer but does not eliminate months already earned under separate qualifying service, and veterans should be able to reach the usual 48-month aggregate entitlement when they have distinct periods of service that independently generate education benefits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues that § 3327(d)(2)(A) supplies the governing formula for determining the amount of Chapter 33 benefits payable to certain veterans who elect Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits, and that the formula applies even when a veteran has multiple periods of qualifying service; under the government’s reading, the statute’s text constrains the payable Chapter 33 entitlement such that these veterans cannot stack entitlements to reach 48 months in the manner petitioner seeks.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to insist we not invoke Brown v. Gardner to conjure ambiguity, and his point that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a specific election/payment formula deserves full weight. But even taking that provision as specific, it does not unmistakably say that independently earned entitlement from separate qualifying service is extinguished, and Justice Thomas’s structural point remains strong: reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) as a hard 36-month ceiling for multi-entitlement veterans would functionally displace § 3695’s express 48-month aggregate framework in the very setting Congress addressed. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Henderson v. Shinseki reinforces my minimalist concern about inferring forfeitures by implication in veterans’ benefits statutes, supporting a narrow holding that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a conversion-calculation rule, not a clear cross-program cap. On institutional grounds, the cleanest path is a limited decision: absent a clear statement, we will not treat § 3327(d)(2)(A) as silently imposing an across-the-board 36-month ceiling where distinct service independently generates additional entitlement subject to § 3695.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a specific, formulaic instruction and that we should not conjure ambiguity to enlarge benefits; but that is precisely why we must read it for what it says—how to calculate what is “payable” under Chapter 33 upon an election—not as an unstated forfeiture of separate entitlement earned under a different statutory program. As the Chief Justice notes, nothing in § 3327(d)(2)(A) speaks with the clarity one would expect if Congress meant to impose a categorical 36‑month ceiling that overrides § 3695’s express 48‑month aggregate-cap rule in the very circumstance where § 3695 matters most. Justice Gorsuch’s Henderson point reinforces my originalist concern with inferring forfeitures by implication: absent unmistakable text, we should not treat a conversion-calculation clause as an implied partial repeal of § 3695. Any residual doubt may be resolved under Gardner, but my conclusion rests on harmonizing the enacted text and avoiding a reading that effectively nullifies § 3695 for multi-entitlement veterans.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take seriously Justice Thomas’s and the Chief Justice’s concern that my reading risks diminishing § 3695’s 48-month aggregate cap in the very cases where multiple entitlements exist. But that argument assumes § 3327(d)(2)(A) is merely another aggregation rule; in context, it reads as a specific election/conversion directive defining what Chapter 33 benefits are “payable” after an election—language naturally operating as a limiting rule for that transactional posture without impliedly “repealing” § 3695 in other settings. Henderson and Brown v. Gardner, pressed by Justice Gorsuch and Justice Sotomayor, do not change that analysis for me because they come into play only once we have genuine interpretive equipoise; here the statute’s payment-calculation text is sufficiently determinate that I will not use canons to create an additional stacking entitlement Congress did not clearly authorize. Given the administrability and fiscal consequences of reading an election provision to permit cross-program stacking beyond the Chapter 33 payable structure, I remain with the Respondent.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to insist we not conjure ambiguity, and § 3327(d)(2)(A) does read like a precise payment-calculation rule for what is “payable” upon election into Chapter 33. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett explain, treating that conversion formula as an implicit forfeiture of separately earned months from distinct qualifying service cannot be squared with § 3695(a)’s express aggregate-cap structure and allocation provisions like § 3322(h)(1), which contemplate distributing different service across different programs. Justice Gorsuch’s Henderson point reinforces that we should be wary of reading veterans’ statutes to impose forfeitures by implication; at minimum, the interaction of these provisions creates genuine interpretive doubt. Under Brown v. Gardner, that doubt—especially where the government’s view would disproportionately harm veterans who served more—must be resolved in the veteran’s favor rather than by importing a clear-statement limitation Congress did not write.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito is right that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is specific and uses “payable” in formulaic terms, so if it clearly imposed a 36‑month ceiling it would control; but read in context, it functions most naturally as an election/conversion calculation to prevent double counting, not as an unmistakable forfeiture of separately earned entitlement from distinct service. Justice Thomas’s structural point that § 3695(a) supplies the express cross-program aggregate cap—and that the Government’s reading would largely drain that 48‑month cap of work exactly where multi-entitlement veterans are concerned—persuades me that Alito’s reading is not the best harmonized textual fit. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers caution underscores that we should not convert a calculation clause into a substantive benefit-cutting limitation absent clearer statutory language, and any residual interpretive doubt is properly resolved for the veteran under Brown v. Gardner (as the Chief and Justice Sotomayor emphasize). Accordingly, I remain with Petitioner on the narrower ground that § 3327(d)(2)(A) does not clearly impose the 36‑month ceiling the Government seeks in the face of § 3695’s aggregate framework.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito is right to insist that a specific statutory formula can control and that Brown v. Gardner cannot be used to conjure ambiguity. But § 3327(d)(2)(A), read in context, most naturally operates as a conversion/payment-calculation rule for what is "payable" under the elected Chapter 33 benefit, not as an unmistakable forfeiture of separately earned entitlement attributable to distinct qualifying service—especially given § 3695(a)’s express 48-month aggregate framework that Justice Thomas and the Chief emphasize. Henderson v. Shinseki reinforces my separation-of-powers concern: we should not infer benefit forfeitures by implication where Congress has not spoken clearly, and we should not let an agency’s administrability/fiscal concerns supply the missing clear statement. If any genuine doubt remains after harmonizing the provisions (as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan outline), Gardner properly resolves it in the veteran’s favor rather than cementing a subset-specific 36-month ceiling not expressed in months-of-entitlement terms.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point remains that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a specific, formulaic instruction for what is “payable” upon a Chapter 33 election and that we should not use Brown v. Gardner to conjure ambiguity. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, reading that payment-calculation clause as a substantive forfeiture of separately earned entitlement from a distinct period of service would work an implied carve-out from § 3695(a)’s longstanding 48-month aggregate-cap framework without a clear statement—an approach that cuts against our usual harmonization and anti-implied-repeal instincts. Henderson v. Shinseki (raised by Justice Gorsuch and echoed by the Chief) reinforces the institutional point that veterans’ benefits statutes are not read to impose forfeitures by implication; that supports treating any genuine uncertainty in the interlocking provisions as resolved for the veteran rather than as an agency-created 36-month ceiling. Administrability and fiscal concerns are relevant, but they cannot supply the missing clear textual command needed to impose the Government’s limiting construction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a specific, formulaic directive about what is “payable” upon a Chapter 33 election and that we should not deploy Brown v. Gardner to create ambiguity. But as Justice Thomas and the Chief explain, the ordinary textual work here is harmonization: § 3327(d)(2)(A) most naturally functions as a conversion/double-counting rule within the election, while § 3695(a) supplies the cross-program aggregate cap when a veteran is entitled under multiple provisions; reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) as an implied 36-month ceiling would largely drain § 3695 of force for the very multi-entitlement cases it addresses. Justice Gorsuch’s clear-statement/separation-of-powers concern underscores that we should not transform a calculation clause into a substantive forfeiture of independently earned entitlement absent unmistakable text. Any residual uncertainty after that structural reading is the kind of interpretive doubt Gardner permits resolving in the veteran’s favor, but my conclusion rests primarily on text and statutory architecture rather than the canon alone.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point remains that § 3327(d)(2)(A) reads like a concrete “payable” formula that could operate as a firm 36‑month limit, and that Brown v. Gardner cannot be used to conjure ambiguity. But as Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan explain, that provision functions most naturally as an election/conversion rule to prevent double counting within Chapter 33—not as an implicit forfeiture of separately earned entitlement tied to distinct qualifying service—especially in light of § 3695(a)’s express 48‑month aggregate framework. Justice Gorsuch’s Henderson v. Shinseki point reinforces my procedural-fairness concern: we should not infer a veteran-harming forfeiture by implication where Congress already provided an explicit cross-program cap and did not unmistakably create a subset-specific 36‑month ceiling. Administrability and fiscal consequences matter, but they cannot supply the clear statement needed to turn a calculation clause into a benefit-cutting limitation that the broader statutory scheme does not clearly endorse.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) is best read as a payment-calculation rule for Chapter 33 elections, not as an implied repeal of the broader statutory scheme that generally permits up to a 48-month aggregate cap when combining distinct GI Bill entitlements. Given the statute’s interaction with that aggregate-entitlement framework, at minimum the provision is ambiguous as to whether it imposes an across-the-board 36-month ceiling for veterans with multiple qualifying periods of service, and that interpretive doubt is resolved in the veteran’s favor under Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115, 117–18 (1994), and King v. St. Vincent’s Hosp., 502 U.S. 215, 220–21 n.9 (1991). A narrow ruling for petitioner preserves Congress’s general 48-month structure while holding only that § 3327(d)(2)(A) does not clearly displace independently earned months attributable to separate qualifying service. That approach respects precedent, avoids reading a silent limitation into veterans’ benefits legislation, and maintains institutional legitimacy by deciding on statutory grounds without broader pronouncements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text and structure of the education-benefits scheme treat § 3695’s 48-month aggregate cap as the controlling limit when a veteran is entitled under more than one VA education program, and nothing in § 3327(d)(2)(A) clearly displaces that aggregate-entitlement rule for veterans with multiple, distinct qualifying periods of service. Section 3327(d)(2)(A) is phrased as a payment-calculation provision tied to an election into Chapter 33, not an across-the-board substantive repeal of previously earned months attributable to separate qualifying service, especially in light of Congress’s express use of aggregate-capping language in § 3695. Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) to impose a categorical 36-month ceiling would render § 3695’s 48-month cap largely superfluous for precisely the class of veterans most likely to have multiple statutory entitlements, contrary to ordinary textualist canons against surplusage. Because the statute does not clearly authorize the Government’s more restrictive result, I would not extend § 3327(d)(2)(A) beyond its text to curtail benefits otherwise permitted up to § 3695’s cap.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) sets out a specific payment-calculation formula governing the amount of Chapter 33 benefits payable upon an election, and its text is best read to cap the payable Post-9/11 GI Bill entitlement at 36 months for the covered class rather than permitting stacking to reach 48 months based on multiple qualifying periods. The veterans’ canon applies only where there is genuine interpretive doubt; under Brown v. Gardner, we do not manufacture ambiguity to expand benefits in the face of a clear statutory formula. Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) to allow veterans to circumvent the Chapter 33 structure by stacking periods of service would undermine the administrability of the election/conversion regime and produce significant fiscal and programmatic consequences that Congress did not clearly authorize. Whatever the broader 48-month aggregate cap in the statutory scheme, § 3327(d)(2)(A) operates as a specific limit on Chapter 33 benefits for these elections and should control absent an unmistakable contrary directive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) is best read as a payment-calculation rule governing how Chapter 33 benefits are computed upon an election, not as an implicit repeal of the broader statutory scheme that generally permits up to a 48-month aggregate cap when combining different GI Bill programs for distinct qualifying service. At minimum, the interaction between § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s formula and the aggregate-entitlement framework creates interpretive doubt, which this Court has said must be resolved in the veteran’s favor. Brown v. Gardner reaffirmed that “interpretive doubt is to be resolved in the veteran’s favor” in veterans-benefits statutes, and King v. St. Vincent’s Hospital likewise directs that “provisions for benefits to members of the Armed Services are to be construed in the beneficiaries’ favor.” Given the real-world stakes for veterans pursuing education and reintegration, I would not read § 3327(d)(2)(A) to cap such veterans at 36 months absent unmistakably clear congressional language doing so.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) is best read as a payment-calculation rule that determines how much Chapter 33 entitlement a veteran receives upon an election/conversion, not as an implicit repeal of Title 38’s broader aggregate-entitlement structure that generally permits up to 48 months when combining distinct GI Bill programs across qualifying service. The government’s reading effectively turns a formula provision into a substantive 36-month ceiling for a subset of veterans with multiple qualifying periods, a significant limitation Congress would be expected to state clearly and to harmonize expressly with the aggregate-cap regime. At minimum, the interaction between § 3327(d)(2)(A) and the 48-month aggregation framework leaves interpretive doubt, which under Brown v. Gardner must be resolved in the veteran’s favor rather than by adopting a constricting construction. That interpretation is also more workable and coherent administratively because it preserves the standard 48-month cap while preventing double counting within a single period of service, instead of creating a special, hard-to-justify carveout for multi-period veterans.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) supplies a payment-calculation rule for Chapter 33 upon election/conversion, but its text does not clearly repeal or override Congress’s separate, generally applicable scheme permitting up to 48 aggregate months of entitlement when combining distinct GI Bill programs; absent a clear statement, we should not read it to impose a categorical 36‑month ceiling even for veterans whose different qualifying service periods independently generate benefits. Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) as a targeted formula (rather than an across-the-board cap) better fits the statutory structure and avoids implying a harsh limitation from silence, especially where Congress elsewhere speaks expressly in months-of-entitlement terms. Any remaining interpretive doubt must be resolved in the veteran’s favor under the pro-veteran canon, which this Court reaffirmed in Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115, 117–18 (1994), and echoed in Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428, 440–41 (2011). In keeping with separation-of-powers principles, the agency may not supply by interpretation a limitation Congress did not clearly enact in the statute’s text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Reading the statute as a whole and in light of longstanding limits on aggregate entitlement, § 3695(a) sets a 48-month cap for receiving assistance under two or more listed GI Bill programs, and nothing in § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s election/conversion calculation clearly overrides that structural limit for veterans who independently qualify under separate periods of service. Related provisions—such as § 3312(a) (establishing up to 36 months of Chapter 33 entitlement based on qualifying service), § 3322(a) (requiring an election but not expressly mandating forfeiture of a distinct entitlement earned from different service), and § 3322(h)(1) (contemplating assigning different periods of service to different programs)—support the practical, workable reading that veterans may use separate entitlements consecutively up to the 48-month aggregate cap. Given the ambiguity created by the interaction of these provisions, the veterans’ canon of construction counsels adopting the interpretation favoring the veteran rather than an implied 36-month ceiling. That approach better respects statutory structure, avoids an atextual forfeiture rule, and aligns with a restrained, precedent- and tradition-based understanding of veterans’ benefits legislation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text and structure of Chapter 33 indicate that § 3327(d)(2)(A) supplies a conversion/payment-calculation rule for the elected Chapter 33 benefit, but does not silently abrogate the separate entitlement a veteran may earn through a distinct period of qualifying service. Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) to impose an across-the-board 36‑month ceiling for all such veterans clashes with provisions that expressly contemplate allocating distinct service to different programs, using entitlements consecutively, and then applying the aggregate 48‑month cap—see 38 U.S.C. §§ 3322(h)(1), 3312(a), 3322(a), and 3695(a). Methodological consistency favors harmonizing these provisions rather than allowing § 3327(d)(2)(A) to render the 48‑month aggregate-cap framework largely ineffectual for veterans with multiple qualifying service periods. To the extent any ambiguity remains after textual analysis, the veterans’ canon supports the veteran-favorable construction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Read in the context of the GI Bill’s broader entitlement scheme, 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) functions as a payment-calculation rule for a Chapter 33 election, not as a clear congressional command to erase or cap months independently earned through separate qualifying service under other programs below the generally applicable 48-month aggregate limit. At minimum, the interaction between § 3327(d)(2)(A) and the statutory aggregate-entitlement framework creates interpretive doubt about whether Congress meant to impose a special 36-month ceiling on veterans with multiple periods of service who would otherwise reach the 48-month cap by combining programs. Under Brown v. Gardner, that interpretive doubt must be resolved in the veteran’s favor, and King v. St. Vincent’s Hospital confirms that servicemember-benefit provisions are construed for the beneficiary when the statutory scheme plausibly supports that reading. This construction also advances procedural fairness and practical consequences by avoiding a counterintuitive penalty for additional service absent unmistakably clear text.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s formula for calculating Post-9/11 GI Bill (Chapter 33) benefits limits a veteran with multiple qualifying service periods to 36 months of education benefits rather than allowing the broader 48‑month maximum available when combining GI Bill programs.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) (calculation rule for Chapter 33 benefits in certain circumstances involving entitlement under another education program), read alongside the statutory framework governing aggregate months of VA education entitlement (including the 48‑month cap across programs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Rudisill argues that § 3327(d) should not be read to strip veterans with multiple, separate periods of qualifying service of education months they otherwise earned under different GI Bill programs; properly interpreted, the statute addresses how to calculate Chapter 33 benefits in specified conversion/election scenarios, not to impose a blanket 36‑month ceiling that overrides the general rule allowing up to 48 total months of combined education benefits for veterans who separately qualify under multiple programs. He and supporting amici emphasize congressional purpose and the long-recognized pro-veteran interpretive principle (the “Veterans’ Canon”) to resolve any ambiguity in favor of veterans’ full benefits.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Secretary contends that § 3327(d)(2)(A) supplies a controlling formula for calculating the payable months of Chapter 33 benefits for veterans who have entitlement under multiple qualifying service periods/education programs, and that the statutory text means the veteran’s remaining/elected entitlement under Chapter 33 is capped such that the veteran cannot receive more than 36 months in the relevant configuration; in the government’s view, applying the formula to multi-period service is consistent with Congress’s design for Chapter 33 elections and prevents stacking beyond what the provision permits.

1943 Supreme Court discussion of liberal construction of veterans’ benefits statutes (referenced generally; specific case name not provided in the excerpt)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s harmonization is the most serious challenge, but it still does not explain what operative work § 3327(d)(2)(A) is doing if § 3695(a) can effectively re-expand Chapter 33 months whenever another entitlement exists—the scenario Congress expressly targeted with an election-and-“remaining” calculation. Justice Thomas’s RadLAX framing best fits my minimalist approach: we should treat § 3327(d)(2)(A) as the specific coordination rule governing this precise election configuration, with § 3695(a) functioning as an outer aggregate ceiling rather than an affirmative grant that alters what “remains” under Chapter 33 after the election. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on the veterans’ canon (Gardner/Henderson) is not enough to move me because, under Arellano, the canon cannot overcome a text-and-structure reading that gives real effect to the targeted coordination provision rather than rendering it largely optional. Absent clearer statutory language authorizing stacking in this election context, I would not adopt a construction that dilutes Congress’s specific formula and raises institutional concerns about judicially expanding benefits beyond the enacted coordination scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s harmonization account is the most serious argument for Petitioner, but it fails textually because § 3327(d)(2)(A) is not merely a conversion metric—it prescribes, in the precise election-and-overlap circumstance Congress addressed, the operative measure of Chapter 33 months “remaining” after the election, leaving nothing for a general aggregate-cap provision to “add back.” Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch say there is no genuine conflict, yet their reading permits § 3695(a) to function as an affirmative source of additional Chapter 33 entitlement whenever another-program entitlement exists, effectively overriding the specific election formula and violating the specific-controls-general principle (RadLAX) as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh explain. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Gardner/Henderson does not move me because, as Arellano reinforces, that pro-veteran tie-breaker cannot be used to dilute a targeted coordination rule when the ordinary textual and structural analysis yields a clear directive. I therefore remain with Respondent: § 3695(a) is an outer ceiling on benefits otherwise authorized, not an independent mechanism to enlarge Chapter 33 months beyond what § 3327(d)(2)(A) specifies in this election context.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s harmonization argument is the best point for Petitioner, but it ultimately depends on characterizing § 3327(d)(2)(A) as mere conversion “accounting” rather than the operative directive Congress wrote for the precise election scenario it singled out—what Chapter 33 entitlement “remains” after the election. As the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas stress (invoking RadLAX and the specific-controls-general principle), reading § 3695(a) to effectively add back months beyond that remaining-entitlement calculation makes the scenario-specific formula optional whenever another entitlement exists, which is hard to reconcile with ordinary structural canons. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on the veterans’ canon does not move me because, under Arellano, it cannot overcome text and structure once the more natural reading is that § 3695(a) is a ceiling on benefits otherwise authorized, not an affirmative source of additional months in the face of § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s election-specific limitation. I therefore would affirm the Secretary’s 36-month result in this election context and leave any broader stacking rule to Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the best case that RadLAX requires § 3327(d)(2)(A) to control in the election scenario and that allowing § 3695(a) to add months would "nullify" Congress’s targeted formula. But that nullification concern assumes § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a categorical cap rather than a Chapter-33 election/conversion computation rule; on the text, it answers how much Chapter 33 entitlement remains after converting, while § 3695(a) separately limits total aggregate entitlement across programs—so both provisions can operate without conflict. Justice Thomas’s view that § 3695(a) cannot enlarge benefits beyond what § 3327(d)(2)(A) grants begs the key question of what § 3327(d)(2)(A) actually grants, and the statute lacks a clear statement that Congress meant election to forfeit independently earned months under other programs. Arellano properly cabins the veterans’ canon, but because ordinary tools still leave real doubt about whether Congress intended that forfeiture-like result, Gardner/Henderson remain an appropriate tie-breaker in the veteran’s favor, especially given the harsh real-world impact on those relying on earned educational benefits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s RadLAX/specific-controls-general point is the hardest pushback, but it only bites if § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s “entitlement … remaining” is the comprehensive cross-program cap rather than a Chapter 33 election/conversion computation. I continue to read § 3327(d)(2)(A) as translating prior usage into what remains of Chapter 33 after the election, while § 3695(a) separately supplies the aggregate ceiling across programs; on that reading there is no true incompatibility and thus no nullification, just two provisions operating at different levels. Justice Roberts’s concern that § 3695(a) would “restore” months misunderstands the mechanism: § 3695(a) caps total benefits but does not refill Chapter 33 entitlement that § 3327(d) has already computed—it simply recognizes independently earned entitlement until the aggregate limit is reached. Arellano, raised by Roberts and Alito, reinforces that we cannot use the pro-veteran canon to override clarity, but here the ordinary tools (text, structure, and avoidance of implied forfeiture) still leave the government’s categorical-cap reading not clearly compelled, so harmonization remains the best textual fit.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Thomas make the best opposing point: under RadLAX, § 3327(d)(2)(A) is arguably the “specific” rule for this election scenario and should control. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, that canon only applies where the provisions genuinely conflict; I still read § 3327(d)(2)(A) as a Chapter 33 election-conversion accounting rule (how much Chapter 33 entitlement is available after electing into it), while § 3695(a) operates independently as an aggregate cap across programs, so both can be given full effect without “restoring” anything or impliedly repealing the 48-month framework. Arellano, invoked by the Chief and Justice Alito, properly limits Gardner, but it does not create clarity where the government’s reading requires treating an election-calculation provision as a silent forfeiture of separately accrued entitlement—an inference I do not find textually compelled. Because harmonization is available and avoids a forfeiture-like construction absent clear statement, any residual doubt is resolved for the veteran.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Barrett’s harmonization argument is the best case for Petitioner, but it still fails my text-and-structure inquiry because it treats § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s scenario-specific directive about what Chapter 33 entitlement “remains” after an election as if it were merely an internal conversion metric that cannot constrain the ultimate months available. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas are right that, in this precise election setting, using § 3695(a) to effectively add back months would largely nullify the targeted limitation Congress wrote into § 3327(d)(2)(A), triggering RadLAX’s specific-over-general principle without needing to find an implied repeal. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Brown v. Gardner (and Henderson) does not move me after Arellano: the veterans’ canon is a tie-breaker only once ordinary tools leave genuine doubt, and here the coordination mechanism Congress enacted resolves the interaction in favor of the narrower, administrable rule. If the forfeiture-like consequence is undesirable policy, that is for Congress to fix by amending the election formula, not for us to reframe the specific directive as non-operative bookkeeping.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s RadLAX-specific-over-general objection is the best case for Respondent, but it still depends on establishing a direct conflict between § 3327(d)(2)(A) and § 3695(a). I continue to read § 3327(d)(2)(A) textually as an election/conversion computation for what Chapter 33 entitlement is available upon election (i.e., how to translate prior usage into the Chapter 33 measure), while § 3695(a) separately supplies an across-program aggregate cap; on that reading, § 3695(a) does not “restore” months that § 3327(d)(2)(A) takes away, it simply limits total benefits otherwise authorized. Justice Thomas’s point that § 3695(a) cannot enlarge benefits beyond what another provision grants is correct as a general matter, but it assumes § 3327(d)(2)(A) is itself a categorical 36-month limiting grant rather than an election-specific accounting rule—an inference I do not find grounded in the provision’s text absent clearer forfeiture language. Arellano, as invoked by Roberts and Alito, appropriately limits the veterans’ canon to genuine ambiguity, but after applying ordinary tools I still think the best harmonized reading avoids treating § 3327(d)(2)(A) as silently displacing the longstanding 48-month aggregate framework.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the RadLAX-specific-over-general argument that § 3327(d)(2)(A) must control in this precise election scenario, but that canon only applies if the provisions cannot be read to coexist; I agree with Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett that they can. On my reading, § 3327(d)(2)(A) performs a Chapter 33 election/conversion calculation (what Chapter 33 entitlement is available upon election), while § 3695(a) operates independently as an across-program aggregate ceiling, so applying § 3695(a) does not “restore” Chapter 33 months so much as prevent an unstated forfeiture of separately earned months under other programs. Justice Thomas’s insistence that § 3695(a) cannot “add” months beyond what § 3327(d) allows assumes the disputed premise that § 3327(d)(2)(A) is a categorical cap rather than a conversion rule, and I do not see clear forfeiture language that would justify that harsh consequence. Arellano properly cabins the pro-veteran canon, but because text and structure still leave genuine doubt about whether Congress meant to silently extinguish independently accrued entitlement, Gardner’s tie-breaking principle remains appropriate rather than outcome-driving.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) sets out a specific formula governing how months of Chapter 33 entitlement are calculated when an individual has entitlement under another VA education program and makes the relevant election, and that specific rule is best read to control over the more general 48-month aggregate-cap framework. Under our cases, the pro-veteran canon is a tool for resolving interpretive doubt, not for overriding a statute’s evident textual and structural limitation; as Arellano v. McDonough explains, the canon “cannot overcome text and structure,” and Brown v. Gardner applies it only where ambiguity remains. Given the statutory coordination mechanism in § 3327(d) and the need for a narrow, administrable rule that respects Congress’s chosen benefit-calculation scheme, I would affirm the Secretary’s application of the 36-month limitation in this configuration. That reading is also consistent with judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy by enforcing Congress’s enacted formula rather than expanding benefits beyond the statute’s terms.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The controlling question is the text Congress enacted: 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) provides a specific entitlement-calculation formula governing the interaction between Chapter 33 and other GI Bill entitlements, and nothing in its terms distinguishes veterans with one qualifying period of service from those with multiple periods. Read alongside the general aggregate-cap provision, the specific formula in § 3327(d)(2)(A) governs this overlapping-entitlement scenario under the settled rule that the specific controls the general. See RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639, 645 (2012). And where statutory language is unambiguous, this Court does not invoke the pro-veteran canon to rewrite the statute; the “cardinal canon” is that Congress means what it says. Connecticut Nat’l Bank v. Germain, 503 U.S. 249, 253–54 (1992).

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The most natural reading of 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) is that Congress prescribed a controlling formula for the amount of Chapter 33 entitlement available when a veteran has entitlement under another VA education program and makes the relevant election, and that formula operates as a cap in the specified configuration rather than a mere bookkeeping provision. Reading § 3327(d) to allow full “stacking” up to the 48-month aggregate maximum would substantially dilute the limiting function of the election-and-calculation scheme Congress enacted for Chapter 33, producing practical consequences (increased payouts and administrative complexity) inconsistent with that structure. The pro-veteran canon does not justify departing from the statute’s evident design where the text and structure point clearly the other way; this Court in Arellano v. McDonough declined to invoke the canon absent genuinely competing plausible readings. Accordingly, I would affirm the Secretary’s application of § 3327(d)(2)(A) as limiting Chapter 33 months in this context to no more than 36 months notwithstanding the broader cross-program maximum.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3327(d)(2)(A) is best read as a targeted calculation rule for specific election/conversion circumstances, not as an across-the-board repeal of the broader statutory framework allowing up to 48 aggregate months of VA education benefits when separate entitlements under different programs are combined. Where the interaction between Chapter 33’s formula and the long-recognized 48-month aggregate cap is at least ambiguous, we must resolve that interpretive doubt in the veteran’s favor under the Veterans’ Canon. Brown v. Gardner reaffirmed that “interpretive doubt is to be resolved in the veteran’s favor,” and Henderson emphasized Congress’s solicitude for veterans and that the system “place[s] a thumb on the scale in the veteran’s favor.” Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) to strip months earned through distinct qualifying service periods would unfairly diminish earned benefits and disproportionately harm veterans who relied on VA’s education programs to reintegrate, contrary to Congress’s remedial design.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Read in statutory context, 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) functions as a calculation rule governing particular election/conversion situations for Chapter 33 entitlement, not as a freestanding override of Congress’s broader framework allowing up to 48 aggregate months of education benefits across VA programs. The Secretary’s reading effectively turns a targeted formula into a categorical 36-month ceiling for veterans who separately qualify under multiple programs, creating an incoherent interaction with the general aggregate-entitlement scheme and making benefits turn on an administratively awkward election mechanic rather than earned service. Where the text and structure reasonably permit either reading, the long-recognized pro-veteran canon favors the interpretation that preserves (rather than silently extinguishes) months of education entitlement earned through distinct service periods. And under Kisor v. Wilkie, agency deference cannot displace the court’s independent duty to apply the best reading of the statute—especially where traditional interpretive tools, including pro-veteran context, resolve the question.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The better reading of 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A), in its immediate context, is that it supplies a conversion/election calculation rule for Chapter 33 in the specified circumstance of switching from another education program—not a freestanding command that overrides the broader statutory framework that generally permits up to 48 aggregate months of education benefits across programs. Nothing in § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s text clearly displaces that separate aggregate-cap regime, and we do not infer such a substantial reduction in earned benefits absent clear congressional direction, particularly given separation-of-powers concerns with agencies creating new limits not grounded in enacted text. To the extent any interpretive doubt remains after applying ordinary tools, the veterans-benefits canon teaches that “interpretive doubt is to be resolved in the veteran’s favor,” Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115, 117–118 (1994), supporting Rudisill’s entitlement to combine separately earned benefits up to the 48-month maximum. Accordingly, I would reverse.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The text and structure of 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) supply a specific calculation rule for Chapter 33 entitlement when a veteran has (or elects) entitlement under another VA education program, and that specific formula should control over more general aggregate-entitlement provisions that otherwise allow up to a 48-month combined maximum across programs. Reading § 3327(d)(2)(A) to permit stacking beyond the formula’s limits would diminish the workability of Congress’s election/conversion scheme and effectively nullify the statute’s targeted restriction in the very circumstances it addresses. Under this Court’s approach, the Veterans’ Canon applies only if there is genuine interpretive doubt after applying ordinary tools of statutory interpretation, see Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115, 118 (1994), and it cannot override clear text and statutory design. Given the specificity of § 3327(d)(2)(A)’s directive, judicial restraint counsels enforcing the enacted formula and leaving any broader expansion of combined benefits to Congress.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually read in context, 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) supplies a calculation rule for a veteran’s Chapter 33 entitlement when the veteran is switching from (or has remaining entitlement under) another listed education program; it does not clearly purport to displace the separate, generally applicable aggregate cap in 38 U.S.C. § 3695(a) that permits up to 48 total months across programs. The government’s reading effectively converts § 3327(d)(2)(A) into a blanket 36-month ceiling for any veteran with multiple qualifying periods of service, but the statute’s operative language is tied to the election/conversion mechanics of § 3327 and does not expressly withdraw months independently earned under different programs for separate service. Applying the specific-over-general canon (RadLAX Gateway Hotel, LLC v. Amalgamated Bank, 566 U.S. 639, 645 (2012)) requires a genuine conflict, and here the provisions can be harmonized by treating § 3327(d)(2)(A) as governing the Chapter 33 computation while § 3695(a) governs the aggregate maximum. Because the best reading avoids implied repeal and gives effect to both limits, I would reverse and hold that the 48-month aggregate cap remains available when separate entitlements are lawfully combined.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Reading 38 U.S.C. § 3327(d)(2)(A) in context, it functions as a conversion/election calculation rule for specified circumstances, not as a clear statement overriding the broader statutory framework that generally permits up to 48 aggregate months of VA education benefits across programs for separately qualifying service periods. Because Congress did not speak with the clarity one would expect before imposing the harsh practical consequence of forfeiting earned months of entitlement based on distinct periods of service, any remaining interpretive doubt should be resolved in the veteran’s favor under the Veterans’ Canon. See Brown v. Gardner, 513 U.S. 115, 118 (1994) (interpretive doubt resolved for veterans), consistent with the Court’s longstanding instruction to construe veterans’ benefits statutes liberally. A pro-veteran reading also better aligns with procedural fairness and real-world reliance interests of servicemembers who reasonably understand multiple qualifying service periods to yield benefits up to the overall cap rather than a program-specific 36-month ceiling absent unmistakable statutory direction.
